II — Probate Research

When an estate can't move forward, the records can

Probate and heir research is forensic genealogy: establishing, with court-ready documentation, who a decedent's heirs are, where they are, and how they are related. We work with the people carrying that responsibility.

AttorneysHeirship research and due-diligence documentation to support filings and affidavits.
Executors & AdministratorsHelp identifying and locating heirs and next of kin when family knowledge runs out.
Trust & Title ProfessionalsKinship research for quiet title, mineral rights, and unclaimed property matters.
FamiliesClear answers about an estate, an inheritance, or a relative no one has heard from in decades.

What a probate research package includes

  • Identification of all heirs at law, with full names, dates, and last known locations
  • A documented kinship chart showing each heir's relationship to the decedent
  • Copies of the supporting records — census, vital, probate, land, and obituary evidence
  • A written report of searches performed, including negative results, suitable for due-diligence files
  • Researcher affidavit support where the court requires it
Please note: The Family Tree Firm provides research and documentation services, not legal advice. Findings are prepared to support your attorney's filings; questions about the law itself belong with counsel.

IV — The Process

From first question to documented answer

  1. 1

    Free initial assessment

    Tell us what you know and what you want to learn. We review your information, tell you honestly whether the records are likely to answer your question, and quote the project in writing before any billable work begins.

  2. 2

    A written research plan

    You approve a plan that names the specific question, the records to be searched, and the repositories involved — so you always know what your research hours are doing.

  3. 3

    Research & analysis

    We search original records online and in person, correlate the evidence, and resolve conflicts between sources — following the Genealogical Proof Standard used by credentialed genealogists.

  4. 4

    Your documented report

    You receive a written report with conclusions, full source citations, and copies or transcripts of key records — plus a pedigree chart where the project calls for one, and clear recommendations for next steps.

V — The Record Landscape

Where the answers actually live

Online indexes are a starting point, not the whole search. A professional project draws on the full range of records your ancestors left behind.

Census & population recordsFederal and state censuses, tax lists, and city directories that place ancestors in a time and place.
Vital recordsBirth, marriage, and death certificates and registers — the backbone of every generation's proof.
Probate & court recordsWills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, and court minutes — often the richest family documents of all.
Land & property recordsDeeds, grants, and plats that track migration, neighbors, and family relationships.
Military recordsService files, pension applications, and draft registrations from the Revolution forward.
Church, cemetery & newspapersBaptisms, burials, obituaries, and local news — frequently the only surviving record of a life.
Immigration & naturalizationPassenger lists, border crossings, and court naturalizations that trace the journey to America.

VII — Questions

Before you ask us to dig in

Very little. A name, an approximate date, and a place — even a family story you're not sure is true — is enough for the free assessment. The form below walks you through exactly what helps; leave blank anything you don't know.

It depends on the records. A focused record retrieval can take days; a multi-generation project or a probate heir search typically runs several weeks, and courthouse or archive requests can add time. Your written quote includes a realistic timeline, and probate cases with court deadlines are prioritized.

A written research report that states the question, the records searched, the evidence found, and the conclusions drawn — with a full citation for every fact, copies or transcripts of key documents, and a pedigree chart where the project calls for one.

No honest researcher can. Records were lost, never created, or are still unindexed — and sometimes the evidence shows a family story isn't accurate. What we guarantee is a thorough, documented search: if the answer can't be found, your report shows exactly what was searched, so the work is never wasted.

Yes. DNA results are evidence, and they work best combined with the paper trail. We can use your matches to test a hypothesis, identify an unknown parent or grandparent line, or confirm a documented line — and explain what the results do and don't prove.

Yes — most probate research is commissioned through counsel, and we are glad to coordinate directly with your attorney, provide documentation in the format the court expects, and support researcher affidavits where required. If you don't have an attorney, we can still help you understand what your family will need.

Yes. Client information and research files are kept confidential and are never published or shared without your written permission. Research involving living people is handled with particular care.
